title: Multimodal AI for bacterial vs viral upper respiratory tract infection multicentre development and internal validation
desc: Distinguishing Group A streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis from viral upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) is critical for appropriate antibiotic use but remains difficult on symptoms alone. We developed and internally validated a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model fusing pharyngeal images (Swin Transformer) with clinical metadata via gradient boosting decision trees, using 6666 visits and 119,988 images from 44 facilities collected March 2023–August 2025. For discriminating GAS from non-GAS (influenza A/B, COVID-19), the fusion model achieved area under the curve (AUC) 0.917 (95% confidence interval 0.907–0.926), outperforming image-only (0.902), metadata-only (0.871) and proxy Centor/McIsaac scores. At a pre-specified high-specificity threshold (≥0.90) sensitivity was 0.761; simulations indicated antibiotic-prescription reductions of 23–56% across GAS prevalences of 5–20%. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed.

title: Social work informatics: an equity framework for health informatics.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Social work informatics (SWI) was proposed as a professional specialty in 2006, yet social work remains under-represented in health informatics governance, research, and system design even as artificial intelligence (AI) shapes high-stakes clinical decisions. This paper introduces the SWI Equity Framework, positioning social work as a leader in designing equitable health informatics systems. The framework was developed through a synthesis of social work, health informatics, and health equity literature. The framework identifies 6 domains: reflexive system co-design, social determinants of health data integration, training-data quality and representation, contextual interpretation of AI outputs, community leadership, and equitable accountability. The framework highlights opportunities to integrate social work expertise throughout the health informatics lifecycle, moving beyond consultation toward active participation in system design, implementation, and governance. It also outlines pathways for advancing social work informatics through education, interdisciplinary research, health systems, and professional infrastructure. Social work is particularly well positioned to advance the equity agenda of health informatics and offers profession-specific expertise that can strengthen equity, accountability, and implementation across the informatics lifecycle.

title: [Articles] Development and external validation of an interpretable machine learning score for early sepsis identification in the emergency department: a multicentre retrospective cohort study
desc: An integer score computed at triage identified ED patients at risk of sepsis with discrimination that transferred across health systems without local re-estimation, supporting its use for risk stratification at triage. Prospective evaluation is needed to establish whether acting on it shortens time to treatment and improves outcomes.

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Shaping the future of venous thromboembolism diagnosis and prognosis.
desc: [Artificial intelligence in medicine] Venous thromboembolism (VTE) continues to pose a substantial health issue worldwide, characterized by high rates of mortality and morbidity. The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has shown potential as a valuable asset for enhancing the detection and prediction of complex diseases, such as VTE. This review explores the role of AI in VTE prediction and diagnosis, analyzing various machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches, including natural language processing (NLP), support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF), logistic regression (LR), gradient boosting methods, and deep learning frameworks such as ClotCatcher. Among the artificial intelligence models, those based on natural language processing algorithms, particularly ClotCatcher, demonstrated strong performance in analyzing unstructured clinical data. ClotCatcher achieved exceptional Area under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.980 and 0.995 for venous thromboembolism (VTE) adjudication from radiology reports. AI-driven methodologies facilitate early detection, personalized risk assessment, and enhanced patient outcomes. AI holds great potential for improving VTE diagnosis and risk assessment, offering greater accuracy and efficiency than traditional methods. However, further studies are required to validate these models across diverse populations and clinical environments. The integration of AI in VTE management represents a promising frontier in personalized medicine, potentially leading to improved outcomes and more efficient healthcare delivery.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
desc: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: Do Clinician-Scored Examples Help LLMs Code ADOS-2 from Hour-Long Transcripts?
desc: Large language models can apply a written rubric to a transcript, making automated coding of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) look within reach. A common way to align such a rater with clinicians is to show it expert-scored examples, but whether correct labels improve agreement is rarely tested. We test this for eight speech-based items of hour-long ADOS-2 Module 3 sessions from 48 children, with one local model and a pre-registered, placebo-controlled design. We compare few-shot scoring, an anchored comparison in which the model only judges a child better, similar or worse than scored anchors and a fixed rule gives the score, post-hoc calibration, protocol-based evidence routing and direct scoring of the full transcript. On 40 held-out children, agreement with clinicians was modest, with quadratic weighted kappa between 0.22 and 0.30. Replacing every example's label with a wrong one changed about a third of the few-shot predictions, more often towards the corrupted labels than chance, but did not lower agreement, 0.25 with correct and 0.23 with wrong labels. A larger second model did the same. The anchored comparison did not improve on few-shot scoring, its cross-child judgements were no more accurate than those implied by absolute scores, and routing did not help. Among the registered, uncalibrated arms, direct scoring of the full transcript agreed best at 0.30. Exploratory follow-up analyses found that the model's graded judgements ranked children better than its final scores, that existing batch calibration raised agreement to 0.46 on the same children, and that in controlled synthetic sessions scoring episodes separately did not beat calibrated whole-transcript scoring. Expert-scored examples do not by themselves calibrate model-based clinical raters, and claims of calibration or added pipeline complexity need corrupted-label controls and strong baselines.

title: XenoType: Decoding cellular identity in breast cancer histology through molecular supervision
desc: Characterizing the cellular composition of the tumor microenvironment from histological images is fundamental to understanding cancer biology and informing treatment decisions. Deep learning has enabled automated nuclear detection and classification from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, yet cell classifiers remain largely confined to broad morphological categories owing to a reliance on manual annotations. Recent efforts have used spatial molecular measurements to supervise histological classification, but these approaches often require separate tissue sections or produce altered H&E staining, and the resulting cell-type annotations depend on subjective choices such as marker selection and clustering parameters. Here we develop XenoType, a framework that classifies cells into seven molecularly informed categories directly from routine histology, trained using paired same-section Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type annotations are reconciled from four single-cell RNA-sequencing references, reducing dependence on marker choices. Across eight held-out breast tissue sections, XenoType outperformed commonly used CellViT++ retrained on the same molecular annotations under both four-class (macro-F1: 0.703 vs. 0.569) and seven-class (macro-F1: 0.571 vs. 0.403) taxonomies, with the largest gains for myoepithelial (F1: 0.175 to 0.572) and endothelial cells (F1: 0.395 to 0.682). Molecular measurements are required only during training; at inference, XenoType uses the H&E image alone. Model-reference agreement increased consistently with annotation confidence, and XenoType generalized to an independently profiled breast tissue section from a different spatial transcriptomics platform, supporting scalable cell-type mapping from routine histology without per-specimen molecular profiling.

title: An Explainable Analytics Framework for Identifying Process Deviations in Emergency Care for Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions
desc: Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions (MLTCs), also known as multimorbidity, often present clinical and operational challenges in emergency departments (EDs), yet how their care pathways deviate from expected workflows remains underexplored. This study introduces a process-aware analytical framework that quantifies and interprets ED process deviations by integrating multi-perspective conformance checking with explainable machine learning. Using routinely collected Scottish ED data between 2017-2023, we derived an empirical benchmark pathway. We introduced a new metric, the deviation score (DS), which captures both structural misalignments and breaches of the four-hour ED standard, a national service target defined as completion of ED care within four hours of arrival. Compared with non-MLTC attendances, MLTC patients exhibited longer and more complex pathways, higher DS values, and lower conformance to the benchmark model. The framework enabled interpretable SHAP analyses, revealing that deviation severity among MLTC attendances was primarily associated with triage acuity, year of attendance, activity queue length (number of patients queuing for the same care activity), and referral source, with additional contributions from age, arrival time, and number of chronic conditions. Threshold effects were observed in both queue length and multimorbidity burden, beyond which deviation severity increased sharply, suggesting points where standard pathways become harder to maintain. These findings show that deviation severity for MLTC patients is shaped by clinical urgency and system-level pressures at presentation. However, the inherent complexity of MLTC patients may further increase vulnerability to deviation. The framework offers the potential foundation for process evaluation and targeted improvement in emergency care.

desc: Dementia risk at any age has been falling for decades. An analysis of ~219,000 people followed for up to 30 years shows that newer generations start old age with a larger cognitive capacity that declines more slowly than that of previous generations, and this combined advantage is large enough to account for the fall in dementia incidence.

title: Potential of multimedia-supported informed consent in clinical practice: a systematic review
desc: Providing targeted, quality-assured patient information is essential for informed and autonomous decision-making but remains resource-intensive when delivered face-to-face. Multimedia-supported informed consent may enhance patient understanding and satisfaction while reducing physician time by complementing, rather than replacing, direct interaction. Our PRISMA-based systematic review, aiming to enable clinicians to implement and evaluate such a supplement, identified 907 articles of which 110 reports from OECD countries were included, including 62 randomized controlled trials. Among studies assessing the outcomes of interest, 71% reported improved patient understanding with multimedia tools compared to standard consent, 41% reported increased patient satisfaction (none reported decreases), and 91% found reduced or unchanged patient anxiety. In synthesis, to the extent possible despite substantial heterogeneity, findings suggest benefits and potential efficiency gains, and we were able to derive recommendations. However, considerable methodological variability and limitations affecting internal validity highlight the need for high-quality head-to-head comparative studies to draw more robust conclusions.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Diagnosis and APOE-Targeted Therapeutics of Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Current topics in medicinal chemistry
desc: [Current topics in medicinal chemistry] Forty to fifty percent of patients have at least one copy of the APOE4 gene mutation, which is the major genetic risk factor for late-onset alzheimer's disease. Risk is increased three to seven times by carrying one copy (heterozygous) and up to twelve to fifteen times by carrying two copies (homozygous). This cognitive decline is linked to impairments in perception, vocabulary, social interaction, and visuospatial performance, as well as alterations in executive function, which affect the capacity to carry out daily tasks. The purpose of this study is to provide comprehensive information on the diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Various search engines like Pub Med, Scopus, Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Elsevier databasesare searched. Progressive loss of memory is the most common symptom of the disease. Advanced medical imaging technologies offer important insights into human anatomy and function. Compounds with mechanisms of action and clinical trials are also incorporated. This also compiles literature on nanocarriers for improved bioavailability. Altogether, 194 studies are included. Amyloid-β plaques are pathologically seeded within the nervous system by APOE, with APOE4 promoting earlier and more prevalent amyloid deposition. Furthermore, by identifying alterations in the brain, Convolutional Neural Networks, a type of deep learning and machine learning technology, have shown an elevated level of precision in diagnosing AD. The Present manuscript has promising therapeutic outcomes, integrating extensive evidence on phytocompounds, nanoparticle-based approaches, and clinical trials. It also highlights key diagnostic parameters and emphasizes the potential of these therapeutic strategies to improve treatment efficacy while minimizing systemic adverse effects.

title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
desc: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

title: A noise-corrected metric for evaluating spatial transcriptomics predicted from histology
desc: Deep learning methods that predict spatial transcriptomics from histology offer scalable molecular profiling of clinical cohorts. However, conventional correlation metrics overstate prediction quality across whole sections by crediting models for recognizing broad tissue regions, and understate fine-scale prediction quality because sampling noise dominates sparse RNA counts. To resolve this, we introduce the reproducible-signal correlation (RSC) metric. RSC randomly splits RNA counts into two halves to separate reproducible signal from sampling noise across spatial scales and within tissue regions or cell classes. Across 12 spot-level and three single-cell methods, RSC revealed that most models capture broad tissue patterns but largely miss differences between neighboring spots or cells, which whole-section correlation overlooks. Within malignant cells, RSC distinguished methods that genuinely capture part of the cell-to-cell heterogeneity from those whose scores across all cells were inflated by cell-type composition. Guided by RSC, we designed a pairwise difference loss between neighboring spots that improved fine-scale predictions on average across 11 models. RSC thus provides a foundation for benchmarking predictions, guiding model design and determining which spatial analyses histology can support.

title: Making Invisible Infrastructure Visible: Data Landscapes Across a National Pain and Opioid Research Network through a Qualitative Assessment
desc: Background Multi-site research networks have become central infrastructure for NIH-supported health research, yet network-level coordination has focused on harmonization, common data models and FAIR principles, while rarely characterizing the heterogeneous data landscapes within a network first. The Helping to End Addiction Long-term(R) Initiative (HEAL Initiative) Data2Action (HD2A) program comprises ten autonomously designed innovation and acceleration projects in opioid use disorder treatment and pain management, with no pre-existing network-level view of what data each project used or how it was governed. Objectives To make the HD2A data-infrastructure landscape visible by systematically characterizing the data environments of all ten projects and identifying cross-project themes, coordination opportunities, and lessons for multi-site networks. Methods Data Infrastructure Support Center staff extracted each project's data-environment characteristics from project documentation into a structured 15-element assessment, which project investigators reviewed and corrected. Two analysts independently coded the ten validated assessments (two-pass inductive content analysis; 19-code codebook), developed six cross-project themes from the coded passages by consensus, and judged each project against them. An investigator reflection survey, summarized descriptively, contextualized the document-based findings. Results Six themes characterized the landscape: all projects integrate multi-source, cross-sector data; dashboards are the common data-to-action venue; adoption of standards-based interoperability is uneven; governance complexity increases nonlinearly with institutional partners; implementation and improvement science frameworks serve as data-quality scaffolding; and sustainability plans depend on institutional transfer. Five synergy clusters were identified. Investigators consistently described data access and governance, not analytic capability, as the binding constraint, and distinguished sustaining technical products from sustaining their use. Conclusions Making a networks data infrastructure visible is not a substitute for harmonization but a prerequisite for deciding how and what to harmonize. HD2As autonomously designed projects share a common structure of constraints, creating opportunities for coordination without uniformity. The structured elicitation approach is replicable in other innovation networks.

title: A systematic review and meta analysis of extended reality interventions for chronic respiratory conditions
desc: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used in rehabilitation but its effectiveness in chronic respiratory conditions remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies comparing XR-based interventions with usual care or alternatives. Searches were performed from inception to March 2025 and risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers. Fifteen experimental studies were included. XR-based interventions significantly improved 6-min walk distance (mean difference [MD] = 29.90 meters), forced vital capacity (MD = 0.37 liters), reduced dyspnea (standardized mean difference [SMD] = −0.61), anxiety (SMD = −2.08), and depression (SMD = −1.10), and improved quality of life (SMD = −1.87). No significant effects were observed for forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted or fatigue. Subgroup analyses showed stronger effects in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and with comprehensive XR programs. Exercise-based XR improved quality of life only, while activities of daily living simulations improved forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted, and nature-based interventions showed no significant benefit. Heterogeneity was substantial, but sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of primary outcomes. XR-based rehabilitation may improve exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life, but larger multicenter trials are required to confirm long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.

title: Beyond Amyloid in Alzheimer's Disease: A Multiscale Evidence-Based Review of Pathogenesis, Biomarkers, and Emerging Therapeutics.
source: PubMed · Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine
desc: [Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine] Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised neuropathologically by amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, phosphorylated-tau neurofibrillary tangles, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal loss. However, the temporal and causal relationships underlying disease initiation, progression, and clinical heterogeneity remain incompletely resolved. Increasing evidence supports a multiscale model in which amyloid-tau pathology intersects with genetic susceptibility, epigenetic regulation, impaired proteostasis, mitochondrial and metabolic stress, neuroimmune activation, vascular dysfunction, and declining neural resilience. Familial variants in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 directly perturb amyloid processing, whereas APOE ε4, TREM2, and polygenic variation influence lipid metabolism, protein clearance, vascular integrity, and glial responses. DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, and non-coding RNAs may further shape neuronal and immune states, although their directionality and causal significance remain incompletely established. Similarly, microbial and environmental exposures have been associated with inflammatory and proteostatic alterations, but definitive evidence for causation in sporadic AD is lacking. This review integrates genetic, epigenetic, proteostatic, metabolic, neuroimmune, vascular, and environmental mechanisms across disease stages and cellular compartments. We critically evaluate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma biomarkers, amyloid/tau PET, multimodal imaging, extracellular vesicles, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approaches for diagnosis, prognosis, stratification, and therapeutic prioritisation. Therapeutic evidence is stratified from established symptomatic treatments and approved anti-amyloid antibodies to investigational tau-, immune-, epigenetic-, RNA-, microbiome-, stem-cell-, neuromodulatory-, and nanoparticle-based strategies. By distinguishing causal human evidence from observational, experimental, and computational findings, this synthesis identifies priorities for biomarker-guided, stage-specific, and mechanism-informed interventions while avoiding premature inference of causality or clinical benefit.

title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
desc: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

title: SYNDRI: Context-aware removal of transcript spillover in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
desc: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution, but imperfect segmentation often misassigns transcripts between neighboring cells, a problem known as transcript spillover. This spillover is niche-dependent and can therefore confound downstream analyses that rely on niche-specific differential expression. True spillover cannot be directly quantified in experimental ST data, so existing correction methods infer contamination indirectly from transcript positions or expression structure. Here we introduce SYNDRI, a post-segmentation correction method that frames spillover detection as a supervised, gene-level classification task. We develop SYNDRI-SIM to generate labeled training data by simulating spillover between spatially mapped scRNA-seq profiles. SYNDRI uses a transformer to predict gene-level spillover probabilities conditioned on each cell's expression, identity, and local neighborhood, without requiring transcript-level coordinates or deconvolution. On held-out simulated data, SYNDRI achieves an AUPRC of 0.86, compared with 0.64 for the next-best method. Across MERFISH, CosMx, and Xenium datasets, SYNDRI achieves the highest aggregate performance across metrics of cell-type separation, reference similarity, and preservation of within-cell-type heterogeneity. In a CosMx lung cancer dataset, SYNDRI removes nearly all potentially contaminating tumor and macrophage markers from differential expression between tumor-associated and stromal fibroblasts while retaining native fibroblast markers. These results demonstrate the utility of learning from simulated spillover to improve the interpretation of spatial gene expression.

Sequential framework for predicting postoperative recurrence and antiseizure-medication withdrawal risk in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
desc: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) is a common drug-resistant epilepsy. Temporal lobe resection is the most effective treatment, but postoperative recurrence and antiseizure medication (ASM) withdrawal remain major clinical challenges. Existing prediction tools are limited by endpoint specificity, restricted external validation, and lack of integration into sequential postoperative management pathways. We developed a sequential modelling strategy in mTLE, spanning recurrence prediction to ASM withdrawal risk stratification. In phase 1, postoperative recurrence models were developed and validated using 52 preoperative multimodal features in 1278 patients across cohorts 1–4 (three retrospective, one prospective). Five top-ranked models achieved AUCs of 0.926–0.932 (internal) and 0.830–0.931 (three external sets), with a three-tier (low/intermediate/high) risk stratification. In phase 2, ASM withdrawal recurrence models were developed and validated in 679 seizure-free, phase 1 low/intermediate-risk patients eligible for withdrawal across cohorts 5–8 (three retrospective, one prospective). Five top-ranked models achieved AUCs of 0.897–0.902 (internal) and 0.789–0.933 (three external sets), with risk stratification for individualized withdrawal estimation. Models showed good calibration, net clinical benefit, and SHAP-based interpretability. A research-based risk-estimation web tool was developed to support potential clinical translation. This promising modelling strategy integrates population-level risk stratification with individualized prediction, providing preliminary postoperative guidance: high-recurrence-risk patients may not be ideal for early ASM withdrawal despite seizure freedom, while low-risk patients may be considered for earlier withdrawal evaluation. Given the primarily retrospective design and relatively small phase 2 prospective cohort, further prospective external validation and clinical-impact studies are required before routine implementation.

title: Artificial intelligence in influenza prevention and control: translational pathways, supporting evidence, and system-level challenges.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
desc: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the π_{0.5} baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the π_{0.5}. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

title: GASTON-VI efficiently quantifies spatial axes and molecular gradients from multi-sample, multi-modal spatial-omics data
desc: Many tissues exhibit an underlying spatial axis along which fundamental biological processes occur due to continuous spatial gradients of cell type and molecular state. Modern spatial-omics technologies measure molecular features (e.g. gene/protein expression) at 100,000s-1,000,000s of locations within a two-dimensional (2-D) tissue slice, with large-scale atlases profiling multiple tissue slices of the same organ type across different individuals and biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). However, existing computational methods for identifying spatial molecular gradients are limited to small spatial transcriptomics datasets (1000s of cells) of a single tissue slice, while methods for integrating multiple samples do not explicitly model spatial axes nor spatial molecular gradients along such axes. Here, we present GASTON-VI, a variational inference (VI)-based deep learning model which efficiently learns an underlying spatial axis and spatial molecular gradients along this axis from multi-sample, multi-condition spatial-omics data of any molecular modality (e.g. transcriptomics, proteomics). GASTON-VI jointly learns (1) a spatial coordinate (the "isodepth") for each individual tissue slice and (2) 1-D spatial modality functions that describe molecular gradients along the isodepth for tissues of the same biological condition, while utilizing a latent variable model to account for batch effects. Further, GASTON-VI implements a statistical test for identifying molecules with differential spatial gradients across biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). On spatial transcriptomics and proteomics data from the intestine, tonsil, and liver, we show that GASTON-VI recovers spatial axes and molecular gradients along these axes more accurately and efficiently than existing methods. In particular, applied to large-scale spatial transcriptomics and proteomics atlases, GASTON-VI reveals differential spatial gradients of gene expression along the portal vein-central vein axis in fibrotic livers, and differential spatial gradients of protein abundance along the muscularis-lumen axis across different regions of the intestine. Software availability: GASTON-VI is available at https://github.com/chitra-lab/GASTON-VI.

Helsinki puts trust at the heart of its smart-city model
desc: Open urban data, recycled data-centre heat and a public AI register are helping the Finnish capital develop responsible urban technology.

title: Transitions of Care in Clinical Oncology: Current Applications and Future Opportunities Enabled by Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health.
desc: [JCO clinical cancer informatics] Transitions of care from hospital to outpatient settings represent a vulnerable period for patients with cancer, who often face complex treatment regimens, multiple comorbidities, and fragmented coordination across care settings. These challenges contribute to communication breakdowns and unplanned hospital readmissions. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies offer new opportunities to improve the transitional phases before, during, and after hospital discharge, and strengthen care continuity. This review examines emerging approaches enabled by AI and digital health across the inpatient-to-outpatient care spectrum for hospitalized patients with cancer. We discuss how predictive analytics and clinical decision support can identify patients at elevated risk of complications and guide discharge planning before hospitalization ends. We also review existing AI and digital health solutions tailored to the discharge process, including tools that enhance patient and caregiver education, medication reconciliation, follow-up coordination, discharge documentation, and management of pending test results. Finally, we explore post-discharge technologies, such as remote monitoring, symptom tracking systems, and AI-assisted communication platforms, that empower earlier detection of clinical deterioration and facilitate integration with outpatient and community-based resources. Overall, we highlight, as well as describe the limitations of, innovations that seek to improve coordination, reduce administrative burden, and support safer, more proactive transitions of care for patients undergoing cancer treatment.

title: VenusPheno: Transfer-Guided Task Grouping for Multi-Task Bacterial Phenotype Prediction
desc: Understanding how genomic information gives rise to bacterial phenotypes is a fundamental problem in biology. Genome-level prediction requires models that integrate information from thousands of proteins, while related phenotypes may share genomic signals. However, not all phenotype tasks benefit from being learned together, and suitable task groups can be difficult to define from biological knowledge alone. We present VenusPheno, a framework that combines multiple-instance learning over pretrained ProtT5 protein embeddings with transfer-guided multi-task learning. An attention-based Set Transformer aggregates the proteins in each genome into a genome-level representation. We evaluate VenusPheno on 14 binary phenotype tasks from 12,178 bacterial genomes using genus-disjoint splits. Under single-task training, VenusPheno outperforms computational, conventional machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines in terms of mean balanced accuracy. We then use leave-one-task-out analysis to estimate directed transfer relationship between phenotypes, revealing both beneficial and detrimental interactions. Grouping tasks based on these transfer relationships further improves mean balanced accuracy over independent training and joint training of all tasks. Although inferred without biological priors, the resulting groups are consistent with biologically plausible relationships among phenotypes. VenusPheno therefore combines accurate phenotype prediction with a data-driven strategy for determining which tasks should be learned together. The PyTorch implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/YJinling/VenusPheno.

title: RadNet's DeepHealth Wins FDA Clearance for AI Breast Cancer Risk Tool
‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
desc: Awe, anxiety and opportunity: mathematics community shares mixed emotions following the solution of the field’s biggest unsolved problem.

title: Artificial intelligence as a tool in primary care practice: From burnout to breakthrough.
source: PubMed · Canadian family physician Medecin de famille canadien
desc: [Canadian family physician Medecin de famille canadien] To provide family physicians with a practical overview of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in primary care practice and their potential to address burnout, improve workflow, support clinical decision making, and enhance patient care. A comprehensive narrative review of AI tools in primary care was conducted using peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, with subject headings artificial intelligence and primary care, along with related terms. Relevant real-world pilot projects and case studies were hand-searched to identify those not captured through database searches. Canadian family physicians are facing rising levels of burnout, driven by overwhelming administrative demands and increasing patient complexity. With 1 in 4 Ontarians estimated to be without a family doctor in 2026, primary care is under considerable strain. AI tools-particularly those powered by natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs)-offer timely, practical solutions across 4 domains: ambient AI scribes to reduce documentation time and enhance patient-physician interaction; intelligent document processing and clinical summarization to streamline inbox management and information retrieval; clinical evidence synthesis LLMs to summarize medical evidence at the point of care; and AI clinical decision support systems to improve diagnosis and disease management. Real-world implementation in primary care demonstrates these tools can improve workflow efficiency, reduce time spent on paperwork, enhance adherence to clinical guidelines, and improve patient satisfaction. However, inaccuracies in AI-generated content, model bias, lack of transparency, and data privacy risks all require careful oversight. AI and NLP applications have potential to be timely tools that reduce strain and restore capacity for relational, person-centred care. Thoughtful adoption-guided by evidence-informed deployment, user-centred design, and regulatory safeguards-will be essential to ensure safe, equitable integration into primary care practice.

title: SPECTRE: A versatile data framework for integrating spectral, environmental, and ecophysiological trait data
desc: With the increasing availability of large datasets and the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI), robust and sustainable data management systems have become essential for plant and ecosystem research. In particular, the integration of heterogeneous spectral data with plant functional traits and environmental measurements from multiple sensors poses a major challenge, requiring significant time investment and long-term planning. Here, we present SPECTRE (Spectral, Trait, and Remote-sensing Ecophysiology data framework), a versatile data framework based on simple, open data formats that addresses the need of many research groups for a standardized organization of heterogeneous datasets, facilitating their integration and joint analysis without relying on proprietary software or external service providers. SPECTRE integrates a wide range of datasets linking spectral measurements to plant traits, including LiDAR, hyperspectral imagery, chlorophyll fluorescence, geospatial data, soil moisture, climate variables, and ecophysiological traits, organized into three main categories: (i) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-acquired data, (ii) ground-based trait measurements, and (iii) environmental data. All datasets are stored using a standardized folder structure and converted to comma-separated values (CSV) format. A unified primary key enables consistent linking of spectral signatures to functional traits across datasets by species and site, facilitating trait-based analyses, data framework extension, and long-term usability. The widespread use of lookup tables reduces data redundancy and facilitates the integration of data with different naming conventions, while the use of Markdown for metadata and documentation ensures easy access to information without relying on complex or proprietary formats, simplifying documentation creation and maintenance. Overall, SPECTRE offers a simple, transparent, and scalable solution that can be readily adopted by plant ecophysiological laboratories, facilitating future AI-driven trait prediction analyses.

title: a2z Radiology Receives FDA Approval of a2z-Omni-Triage
Clinical decision support for precision dentistry: Trends and emerging prospects.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)
desc: [Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)] Precision oral health requires clinicians to consider patient-specific clinical, biological, behavioral, imaging, and preference sensitive data when making clinical decisions. In routine oral health care, however, these data are often fragmented across electronic dental records, imaging platforms, diagnostic tests, narrative notes, and patient-generated sources. Clinical decision support (CDS) systems provide a mechanism for organizing these data and translating them into timely, evidence-informed recommendations at the point of care. A narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed literature relevant to precision dentistry, CDS, dental informatics, artificial intelligence, biomarkers and omics technologies, and patient-generated health data. Priority was given to dental studies, which were supplemented by broader medical CDS literature when dental-specific evidence was limited. CDS systems can function as digital infrastructure and generate clinical recommendations based on patient-specific data using evidence-based knowledge and predictive analytics. In dentistry, CDS applications range from rule-based reminders and electronic quality measures to artificial intelligence-assisted radiographic interpretation, risk prediction, biomarker screening, and emerging multimodal platforms. The clinical readiness of these technologies varies substantially, and their value depends on data quality, validation, work flow integration, usability, interoperability, privacy safeguards, and clinician oversight. CDS systems can assist clinicians by offering evidence-based, personalized recommendations that synthesize pertinent and available information. These systems are crucial for practicing precision dentistry. Although efforts to enhance the adoption, usability, effectiveness, and acceptance of CDS systems continue, clinicians should always regard CDS systems as tools and retain full responsibility for their decisions and involve patients in the decision-making process.

title: Does embedding impact classification performance ? A small sample perspective
desc: Deep learning (DL) methods can address many challenges posed by high-dimensional and sparse microbiome data. In this study we applied and compared deep (DNN) and shallow (SNN) feedforward neural networks combined with five dimensionality-reduction techniques: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), Autoencoder based Embeddings (AE), and convolutional layers (Conv). To establish baseline classification performance, the XGBoost was used, as it represents a robust machine learning based classifier with a relatively low number of hyperparameters. The task was to classify effective microorganism (EM) treatments based on intestine bacterial family abundance in common carp. In particular, the experiment involved 25 ponds that were divided into experimental groups. In each pond, the intestinal microbiome of five individuals was determined by sequencing two hypervariable regions of the gene encoding the 16s rRNA gene sequencing. The sequence reads were processed by QIIME2 and taxonomically annotated to the SILVA database, what resulted in 126 annotated families that were used as features in all downstream analyses. Abundance tables from 125 samples, transformed using the Centered Log-Ratio (CLR) method, were used to evaluate ten dimensionality-reduction and Deep learning configurations considering five-, three-, and two-classification scenarios. The DL models were optimized using cross-validation. To combat the overfitting that was present due to sparsity and small sample size, dropout and kernel regularization were implemented. During testing autoencoder embeddings achieved the highest classification accuracy (0.84), exceeding the XGBoost baseline (0.64), while embedding based on convolutional layers significantly reduced performance (0.44). PCA and SVD transformations showed comparable results (0.65), whereas NMF often failed to converge, likely due to incompatibility with CLR-transformed data. Best classification results were obtained for models that implemented AE embedding, it is most likely caused by their ability to capture non-linear patterns in the data. All models showed stable training behavior, with loss functions consistently decreasing across epochs. The SNN models were markedly less computationally intensive, than DNN. Radiomics is not dead: quantitative imaging in the era of deep learning in renal cell carcinoma.
desc: [Frontiers in oncology] A growing consensus in the imaging community holds that radiomics has been rendered obsolete by foundation models and end-to-end deep learning. We disagree, and this perspective explains why. The critics are partially right: inter-operator segmentation variability has compromised reproducibility, methodological quality has been inconsistent, and the gap between published AUCs and clinical implementation has been wide. However, they draw the wrong conclusion. In renal cell carcinoma (RCC), where preoperative contrast-enhanced CT is already standard of care for every patient undergoing nephrectomy and where approximately 30% will recur after surgery, radiomics remain an immediately actionable, interpretable, and deployable non-invasive prognostic tool available. We argue that its primary technical limitation (segmentation variability) is being eliminated by the same deep learning technology used to argue against it: automated segmentation frameworks such as nnU-Net achieve Dice coefficients exceeding 0.93 on external cohorts, removing inter-operator noise. We further argue that in low-prevalence, high-stakes oncological settings, the data volumes required to pre-train foundation models do not exist, and that interpretability - now a regulatory requirement under the EU AI Act for high-risk clinical AI systems - is native to handcrafted radiomics and must be retrofitted onto deep learning architectures. Most critically, we present biological evidence that CT images encode tumor microenvironmental and molecular information invisible to the human eye. This generates a directly testable hypothesis: that preoperative radiomic scores can predict not only recurrence but also likelihood of benefit from adjuvant treatment. Radiomics is not dead. It is, at last, being done properly.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Detection of Tumor Calcification in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Emerging Opportunities in Computational Oral Pathology and Biomineralization Research.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Objective: Tumor-associated calcification is increasingly recognized as a potentially relevant feature of the tumor microenvironment across multiple malignancies; however, its significance in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly understood and is frequently overlooked during routine histopathologic assessment. This perspective examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted computational pathology to improve the detection, quantification, and spatial characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and discusses its potential as an emerging histopathologic research phenotype and candidate biomarker requiring further validation. Design: A narrative synthesis of the current literature was undertaken to evaluate the biological mechanisms underlying tumor-associated calcification in OSCC, recent advances in biomineralization research, and the application of AI and computational pathology in digital histopathology. Current evidence was integrated to propose future AI-based workflows for objective calcification assessment and to identify opportunities for investigating its potential biological and clinical relevance. Results: Current evidence indicates that calcification has been reported or proposed in vascular, stromal, necrotic, and extracellular matrix-associated contexts in OSCC and related pathological settings; however, the prevalence, biological mechanisms, and reproducibility of these patterns in OSCC remain insufficiently characterized. Potential associations with hypoxia, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and osteogenic-like cellular reprogramming are supported primarily by evidence from broader biomineralization, vascular calcification, and other tumor contexts rather than by calcification-specific mechanistic studies in OSCC. Advances in whole-slide imaging, deep learning, and computational pathology have enabled automated tissue segmentation, feature extraction, and quantitative histopathologic analysis. However, their application to the systematic detection and spatial characterization of calcification in OSCC remains limited. AI-assisted analysis could facilitate objective identification, quantification, and spatial mapping of mineralized structures, providing a conceptual research framework for investigating tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental remodeling. title: Explainable CNN Ensemble with AI-Generated Reporting for Fungal Infection Diagnosis.
desc: [Journal of fungi (Basel, Switzerland)] The need for precise classification of fungi from microscopic images plays a critical role in diagnosing and treating patients since it requires timeliness and effectiveness. Nevertheless, manual examination is time-consuming and difficult due to the similar visual features of numerous fungi. Therefore, this work proposes a new approach to explainable deep learning for fungal image classification and report generation. The developed framework consists of four pre-trained convolutional neural network models-DenseNet121, ResNet18, VGG16, and InceptionV3-which are used to classify fungal microscopic images into five classes. To make the process more transparent, methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and Canny edge detection are used to identify the areas of images that contribute to the prediction. At the same time, the developed approach uses the large language model LLaMA3-70B through LangChain and provides automatic generation of the structured diagnostic report, including fungal identification, confidence scores, and clinical observations. The whole pipeline is implemented using the Streamlit interface to predict and generate a PDF report of the classification. The experiments have been performed using publicly available data containing 5000 images of fungi with expert annotations. Among the models analyzed, DenseNet121 shows the highest result, reaching an accuracy of 99.75% and having the values of precision, recall, and F1-score close to 0.998.

title: Marine Natural Products for Cancer Therapy: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Translation.
desc: [Marine drugs] Cancer continues to impose a major global health burden. Conventional therapies often show poor selectivity, off-target toxicity, and drug resistance, creating an urgent need for new agents. The marine environment covers roughly 71% of Earth's surface and has fostered metabolites of unparalleled chemical diversity, making the ocean a vital source for anticancer drug discovery. This review critically examines the published literature on six representative marine-derived agents-cytarabine, trabectedin, eribulin, brentuximab vedotin, carrageenan, and Aspergillus fumigatus alkaloids. We compare their biological sources, anti-tumor spectra, molecular targets, and oncogenic pathways, and we analyze the structure-activity relationships and the total, semi-, and engineered synthesis routes that underpin their optimization. We also appraise the major barriers to clinical translation-sustainable supply, mechanistic ambiguity, and suboptimal druggability-alongside emerging solutions based on synthetic biology, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and advanced formulation. Marine-derived agents therefore represent a chemically distinctive and mechanistically diverse reservoir for targeted cancer therapy. Realizing this potential will require structure-activity-guided optimization, secure synthetic or engineered supply, and biomarker-informed combination strategies that still await prospective validation.

title: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Risk Stratification: Current Evidence and Emerging Approaches.
desc: [Current oncology (Toronto, Ont.)] Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is characterized by marked biological and clinical heterogeneity that is only partly captured by conventional anatomical staging. This narrative review examines how circulating biomarkers, radiomics, artificial intelligence (AI), molecular profiling, and functional tumor models may complement tumor-node-metastasis (TNM)-based risk stratification in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Relevant literature was identified through searches of PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, primarily covering 2016-2026, with earlier landmark studies retained when relevant. Plasma Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA is an established prognostic biomarker that complements anatomical staging, while longitudinal measurements provide information on treatment response and recurrence risk. Radiomics and AI offer additional possibilities for prognostic modeling, although their use in treatment selection remains investigational. Genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic studies characterize tumor and microenvironmental heterogeneity. Organoids, xenografts, humanized models, and engineered three-dimensional systems provide complementary platforms for functional investigation.

title: Data drift in clinical imaging AI: Medicolegal liability after deployment.
desc: [Clinical imaging] Data drift refers to changes in the distribution or characteristics of input data after deployment that may adversely affect the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, even when the software continues to function exactly as designed. Patient demographics, disease prevalence, referral patterns, imaging protocols and technology continue to evolve after deployment, resulting in a divergence between the data distribution a model was trained on and the distribution it encounters in practice, without any discrete coding error or malfunction. These technical realities raise distinctive medicolegal questions when a patient is harmed by a degraded model. Establishing negligence centers on whether an ongoing institutional duty exists to monitor for performance deterioration, how breach can be proved absent consensus benchmarks for surveillance frequency and how causation can be demonstrated where AI output is only one element of clinical decision-making and its reasoning may be an opaque "black box" to its users. Comparative fault principles may allocate responsibility according to relative control and knowledge among institutions, vendors and radiologists. Products liability exposure and federal preemption laws also play a role. Risk reduction measures include lifecycle documentation, risk proportionate surveillance, auditability of algorithms and outputs, contractual allocation of monitoring responsibility, and sustained clinician oversight. Radiologists and institutions should anticipate a standard of care that evolves well before controlling case law develops.

title: The role of Artificial Intelligence in food allergy: A framework for navigating novel tools.
desc: [Journal of food allergy] Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly penetrated health care and begun to influence clinical care, research, and health system operations. With food allergy, AI offers promise for clinical decision support, personalized care guidance, support of health literacy and a drive toward novel therapies. Despite growing enthusiasm, there are currently no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-cleared AI tools specifically indicated for food allergy, which underscores the need for a structured approach for evaluating, selecting, and implementing AI solutions within the domain. This narrative review focuses on a pragmatic framework for AI tool selection tailored to food allergy use cases. I review the current state of AI in health care and allergy/immunology, describe key dimensions of tool selection, including clinical question definition, data suitability, performance trade-offs, user interaction, governance, and sustainability, and illustrate how these considerations may be applied to food allergy-relevant challenges. By shifting attention from model novelty to problem-solution fit, implementation readiness, and long-term stewardship, this framework aims to support clinicians, researchers, and health systems to responsibly leverage AI for improved patient outcomes.

title: AI-driven transformation of GPCR research: from structural biology to precision medicine.
desc: [Frontiers in molecular biosciences] G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) regulate complex pathophysiological networks and represent a critical class of drug targets, but their structural determination and ligand screening are constrained by dependence on homology templates, static conformations, and a bias toward known ligands. Artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming GPCR structural biology and pharmacology by overcoming these bottlenecks. The methodologies encompass high-precision static structure prediction, dynamic conformational ensemble modeling, ultra-large-scale virtual screening, de novo ligand design, allosteric mechanism decoding, biased signaling quantification, and systems pharmacology. Deep learning architectures enable end-to-end structure prediction exemplified by AlphaFold series, billion-compound virtual screening and unbiased de novo ligand design via diffusion models. Three-dimensional structure-aware Graph neural networks and molecular dynamics simulations are shifting research focus from single static conformations to transient conformations, cryptic allosteric sites, and ligand-induced biased signaling. Systems-level investigation through multi-omics-integrated GPCR digital twins advances personalized precision medicine. This review summarizes the innovative AI-driven paradigm, breaking traditional restrictions and greatly improving structural resolution of orphan receptors and GPCR complexes, thereby offering a comprehensive reference for dynamic GPCR pharmacological research. Core challenges include the black-box nature of deep learning, structural distribution biases, and the translational gap, which can be addressed by physics-informed models and high-throughput validation.

title: Choosing the Right AI Model for Uveal Melanoma From Detection to Prognosis.
desc: [Clinical & experimental ophthalmology] Ocular oncology sits in an unusual position for medical artificial intelligence (AI), imaging heavy and multimodal by nature, but constrained by the rarity of the tumours it treats. Uveal melanoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, accounts for approximately 7095 new cases worldwide each year. Choroidal naevi are present in approximately 5% of the white population aged 40 and over, of which roughly 1 in 8845 transforms into melanoma each year, leaving a large benign population within which a small number of melanomas must not be missed. This narrative review follows the uveal melanoma clinical pathway through detection, diagnosis and prognosis, asking at each stage which class of AI model the evidence supports. A structured PubMed search returned 176 unique records, from which 29 primary studies were included, 17 (59%) published in 2025 or 2026. At detection, heavy self-supervised foundation models generalise well across imaging hardware but lack calibration to a clinical decision, while lightweight purpose-built classifiers show the opposite trade-off, and only one tool has been tested in a real referral workflow, quadrupling the odds of correct referral and cutting false positives 10-fold. At diagnosis, purpose-built convolutional classifiers calibrated to a referral threshold remain most mature, reaching 0.88 AUC on two cohorts, while multimodal fusion claims rest on a single 0.01 AUC gain. At prognosis, biomarker prediction from routine pathology reaches 0.93 to 0.99 AUC, survival prediction lags, only 7 of 29 studies (24%) had external validation and none of the tools has regulatory clearance.

title: An Alert Is Not a Referral: Toward Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning in Gastric Cancer Screening.
source: PubMed · Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology
desc: [Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology] Accurate identification of near-fall events is essential for early fall-risk assessment and prevention in older adults. However, translating laboratory-trained machine learning algorithms into real-world settings remains challenging because abnormal gait patterns do not necessarily represent genuine near-fall events. This correspondence highlights the distinction between sensor-detected gait perturbations and clinically meaningful losses of balance, emphasizing the limitations of conventional signal-based classification and the absence of event-level validation. We propose a context-grounded multimodal framework integrating wearable sensor data with large language model-derived information from patient narratives, caregiver reports, and clinical documentation. Such integration could support contextual event interpretation, distinguish habitual gait instability from transient balance disturbances, and facilitate clinically adjudicated near-fall identification. We further emphasize the importance of prospective validation, uncertainty-aware prediction, subgroup fairness, and clinically relevant performance metrics. Advancing from isolated movement classification toward context-aware, clinically validated event detection may improve individualized fall-risk prediction and support more effective preventive interventions in geriatric care.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Exercise Prediction, Monitoring, and Personalization: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
desc: [Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology] Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to physiological prediction, physical activity monitoring, and personalized exercise prescription. However, evidence regarding its practical effectiveness remains heterogeneous. This systematic review examined applications of AI, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) in exercise-related prediction, monitoring, and personalization among adults. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2025, with Google Scholar used as a supplementary source. Eligibility followed PICO: adults aged 18 years or older (P); AI, ML, or DL applications for exercise prediction, monitoring, or personalization (I); conventional or non-personalized approaches, where applicable (C); and predictive accuracy and physiological, functional, or behavioral exercise outcomes (O). Findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: Ten studies were included: four examined physiological or energy-expenditure prediction, two investigated activity-related behavioral outcomes, two evaluated training-response classification or recommendation generation, and two assessed AI-personalized exercise interventions. Predictive models demonstrated promising performance in specific applications, although validation procedures and populations varied substantially. The intervention studies reported greater perceived exercise intensity and satisfaction in one trial and improvements in selected measures of balance, flexibility, and strength in another. Conclusions: AI-based approaches show potential for supporting exercise assessment, monitoring, and individualized decision-making. However, evidence regarding their superiority over conventional exercise prescription remains limited by the small number of intervention studies, methodological heterogeneity, and insufficient external validation. Further well-designed, long-term intervention studies are needed to establish their comparative effectiveness and practical benefits.

title: AI-Driven Dual-Graphene Near-Infrared SPR Biosensor for Non-Invasive Salivary Cortisol Monitoring.
desc: [Biosensors] Non-invasive salivary cortisol measurement requires separation of receptor binding from matrix effects and measurement artefacts. We combined a 1550 nanometre dual-graphene optical transducer with an antibody-functionalised cortisol assay and two separately evaluated artificial intelligence workflows. For structural modelling, 8192 scrambled Sobol proposals yielded 7941 accepted geometries. Grouped development selected an extremely randomised tree ensemble, whose sealed-test coefficient of determination was 0.986. Genetic and particle swarm searches were performed after model freeze, and direct transfer-matrix calculations gave a leading candidate sensitivity of 198.60 degrees per refractive-index unit and a resonance width of 0.1790 degrees. These computational candidates were distinct from the nominal cartridge used experimentally. The receptor-functionalised assay had a detection limit of 0.15 nanograms per millilitre and a validated quantitative range of 0.25-8.00 nanograms per millilitre. A gradient-boosted model using complete target and reference angular traces achieved mean absolute errors of 0.25 and 0.50 nanograms per millilitre in 25 blinded artificial-saliva samples and 40 human-saliva samples, respectively; conventional calibration gave corresponding errors of 0.34 and 0.62. Human-saliva measurements were compared with isotope-dilution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Nominal 90% prediction intervals achieved 92% and 90% coverage. The nominal optical advantage over the simpler AZO/graphene reference was incremental, and residual cortisone cross-reactivity remained. These results support a proof-of-concept biosensor requiring further manufacturing and external clinical evaluation.

title: Can AI Accurately Estimate Nutrition From a Food Photo?
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Nutrition tracking can be a useful tool for achieving health and fitness goals, and AI photo features may help alleviate some of the burden of tracking food manually. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Anna Zucker reports on the accuracy and potential trade-offs of these new AI features.

title: Evidence-Grounded Artificial Intelligence for Implant Treatment Planning: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of RAISE.
desc: [Journal of periodontal research] RAISE is an evidence-grounded, retrieval-augmented AI system integrating domain-specific evidence retrieval and structured clinical reasoning for implant treatment planning. In preliminary evaluations, RAISE-generated and RAISE-assisted resident treatment plans received higher expert ratings than their respective comparators, while RAISE assistance was associated with shorter planning time.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Mandibular Growth-Rotation Phenotypes from Lateral Cephalometric Radiographs: A Comparative Evaluation of Convolutional Neural Networks.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Background/Objectives: The cross-sectional classification of mandibular growth-rotation morphology is relevant to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, but conventional structural assessment is observer-dependent. This study developed and internally evaluated deep learning models for classifying existing clockwise and counterclockwise mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes on lateral cephalometric radiographs; it did not forecast future longitudinal growth. Methods: Eight hundred untreated radiographs from individuals aged 9-20 years were labelled by consensus using Björk and Skieller morphological indicators (clockwise, n = 376; counterclockwise, n = 424). A stratified 80:20 training-validation split was used. ResNet50, InceptionV3, and VGG16 were fine-tuned after Gaussian noise reduction, min-max normalisation, and limited geometric augmentation. Results: VGG16 showed the most favourable validation accuracy-loss profile. The archived aggregate confusion matrix (n = 800) yielded an apparent accuracy of 81.13% (95% CI, 78.38-83.75) and balanced accuracy of 81.32% (95% CI, 78.62-83.96); recall was 84.57% for clockwise and 78.07% for counterclockwise phenotypes. Because the matrix included the complete labelled cohort, these values are descriptive apparent performance and not an independent test estimate. Conclusions: VGG16 can classify cross-sectional mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes with promising apparent performance. External, longitudinal, and observer-benchmark validation is required before clinical use.

title: GRLV: Gradient reversal layer with variance loss for major depressive disorder detection.
desc: [Journal of neural engineering] Deep learning models have been widely applied to predict major depressive disorder (MDD) using magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. However, these models often suffer from limited performance and generalization. This is primarily due to the strong individual heterogeneity inherent in MEG temporal signals, which makes it difficult for models trained on small samples to distinguish disease-related features and individual-specific features. To address this issue, we propose GRLV, a plug-and-play framework based on gradient reversal layer with variance loss, that can be readily embedded into existing deep learning classification models. This framework introduces a variance loss function to the gradient reversal layer (GRL) framework to compensate for its convergence limitations. We evaluated GRLV on 10 backbone models, achieving an average classification accuracy of 68.2%, and surpassing baseline models by 3.5%. Visualization results prove that the GRLV framework effectively attends to bilateral occipital activities within the first 100 ms post stimulus on-set, which is associated with the early processing of negative emotional faces in MDD patients, and is a better disease marker due to less contamination from individual heterogeneity. These findings fully demonstrate the broad application potential of GRLV in existing MEG/EEG decoding models and the discovery of mental diseases. These findings fully demonstrate the broad applicability of GRLV on existing MEG/EEG decoding models and its potential for advancing the discovery of biomarkers of mental disorders.
